title: Discrete Diffusion VLA
one_liner: Instead of generating robot actions all at once or in a left-to-right sequence, unroll the action generation like denoising: start with all action slots hidden, then reveal the most confident ones first, then the harder ones, allowing the model to self-correct uncertain predictions.
lead: Vision-language-action models teach robots to follow instructions by combining image understanding with language. Today they either predict actions one token after another in fixed order (slow and inaccurate) or bolt a separate diffusion module onto the side (which breaks the shared visual-language understanding the model learned before). This paper puts discrete diffusion directly inside the model backbone, letting the model predict all action parts in parallel but adaptively, revealing the actions it is most confident about first and leaving room to refine the shaky ones.

problem.h2: Two bad ways to teach robots to act
paras: A robot needs to understand a picture and a spoken instruction, then output a sequence of movements: move the arm, rotate the wrist, open the gripper. Large vision-language models are great at understanding images and text, so it makes sense to build on them.

But these models were trained to predict text one token at a time, left to right. If you force them to predict robot actions the same way, they get stuck: the first action token has almost no context (it does not know what the rest of the action will be), so it guesses poorly. By the time later action tokens appear, the earlier mistakes are locked in.

To fix that, researchers added a separate diffusion module: instead of predicting actions inside the language model, they bolt on an extra piece that generates actions from scratch. But now the model has two competing goals—understand images and language on one side, generate actions on the other—and they pull in different directions. The result: the model forgets the visual and language skills it had learned before. On out-of-distribution tests (when the robot sees something different from training), performance crashes.

callout.html: The paper keeps the action generation inside the shared vision-language model but changes how it predicts: instead of guessing each action token blindly, it iteratively unmasks tokens—revealing confident action parts first, then refining uncertain ones—so the whole model stays aligned and vision-language understanding survives.

panels.title: 1. The old way: left-to-right
panels.caption: Action tokens guessed one by one, early ones blind.

panels.title: 2. The problem bites
panels.viz_args: Error cascades; poor first guess locks in mistakes.
panels.caption: Errors propagate left to right; vision-language skills erode.

panels.title: 3. The paper's move: mask all, then unmask
panels.caption: Start: all action tokens hidden. Model sees picture, language, nothing yet.

panels.title: 4. Reveal confident ones first
panels.caption: Unmask high-confidence actions in early steps; hard ones stay masked.

panels.title: 5. Refine uncertain parts last
panels.caption: Later steps refine shaky predictions; full context now available.

steps.text: Convert each robot action (move arm 5 cm, rotate wrist 30 degrees, open gripper) into small integer tokens (like binning continuous values).
Group H consecutive timesteps of actions into one fixed chunk (e.g. 12 timesteps, each with 7 tokens, making 84 action tokens total).
Hide all 84 action tokens. Feed the picture and instruction to the transformer; it sees everything except the actions.

In each of T steps (e.g. 4 steps), unmask fewer tokens. Step 1: keep most masked (reveal ~25%). Step 2: reveal more (~50%). Steps 3–4: refine the rest. The model predicts masked positions using the unmasked actions plus image and language as context.

Do not unmask randomly. Let the model's confidence guide the schedule: tokens the model outputs with high certainty in early steps get unmasked first (the easy ones), because predicting them correctly gives the model trustworthy anchors; tokens with low certainty stay masked longer (the hard ones), so later steps can use those anchors to narrow down the possibilities, making hard predictions more accurate.

paras: The paper changes how robot actions are generated: from a fixed left-to-right sequence inside a language-model head to a masked-token prediction loop inside the shared transformer backbone, with bidirectional attention (each action token can see all language, image, and other action tokens).

hidden.h2: Mask ratio: how many action tokens to hide at each step
hidden.name: Mask ratio schedule (gamma)
paras: During training, for each batch of actions, the paper samples a mask ratio—a fraction of tokens to hide—from a schedule that follows a predictable curve. This mimics diffusion: early in training, many tokens are masked (learning happens through full context); later, fewer tokens are masked (learning gets refined).

During inference (when the robot actually acts), the model starts with everything masked and follows a fixed schedule: step 1 might mask 100% of action tokens, step 2 might mask 75%, step 3 might mask 50%, step 4 might mask 25%. High-frequency, easy-to-predict tokens get unmasked early (revealed in steps 1–2); low-frequency, harder tokens stay masked longer (refined in steps 3–4). The paper learns this adaptive order implicitly: the model outputs are higher-confidence for some dimensions, and the schedule naturally favors revealing those first. If later the model sees it made a mistake (step 4 output conflicts with step 1 output), it can re-mask uncertain tokens and try again—this is called secondary re-masking.

heat.caption: Darker means higher confidence in early steps. Marked tokens are revealed first; faint ones stay masked longer.

reads.html: Mask ratio is just: how many action tokens to hide right now. A schedule tells you this number at each step. Early steps hide most (model learns rough shape). Late steps hide few (model refines details). It is like sketching: you draw the outline first (confident lines), then shade in (refinements).

The paper uses a decreasing mask schedule where each step t has a lower mask fraction than the previous step. During training, the mask fraction is drawn from a predictable curve. During inference, the mask fraction decreases in a fixed sequence. The model learns which dimensions are easy (high confidence early) and which are hard (require later refinement) from the training objective.

mechanism.h2: Why this fixes both problems at once
paras: The core difference: the model does not need to guess actions in one forward pass, and it does not need a separate diffusion head. Instead, it can refine iteratively using the full model context.

Mechanism 1 (stays aligned with vision-language): The paper trains with only masked cross-entropy loss—the same loss that trained the original language model. There is no auxiliary objective, no competing signals pulling the model in two directions. The model learns to predict masked action tokens using vision, language, and unmasked action tokens as context, all inside the same model. Because the loss objective never contradicts the original vision-language training, the model does not unlearn those skills.

Mechanism 2 (adaptive order is more efficient): In early steps, the model confidently predicts easy action dimensions (e.g. gripper open/close is binary and obvious from the image) because they have few degrees of freedom and visual answers. In later steps, it refines harder ones (e.g. exact arm position requires subtle language reasoning, translating instruction phrases into coordinates). By masking in decreasing quantities, the model can use each earlier prediction to inform later ones—if the gripper is open, the arm position predictions can be narrower—making final refinement more accurate and faster than guessing all actions at once.

Mechanism 3 (secondary re-masking allows self-correction): After step 4 is done, if the model detects internal contradiction (a gripper state that conflicts with the arm position, or actions that violate physics), it can re-mask uncertain tokens and refine them. Because the model sees all predictions at once (they are all outputs from the same step), it can check consistency across action dimensions; if two conflict, the lower-confidence one gets re-masked and refined. This adds a consistency-checking loop that vanilla parallel decoding cannot do, because single-pass methods have no way to revise.

math.h2: The training objective in one equation
math.words: Cross-entropy loss on masked action tokens. Sample a mask ratio from a schedule, hide that fraction of tokens, train the model to predict what is hidden given what is not hidden.
math.equation: L = -sum_i [1_{i in mask} * log P(a_i | unmasked_actions, image, language)]
symbols: 1 if token i is masked, 0 if visible
the true action token at position i
probability model assigns to the correct token given visible context
the action tokens that are NOT masked

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the model outputs probabilities: P(arm_x = 42) = 0.8, P(gripper_open = 1) = 0.6.
Total for those two tokens: 0.22 + 0.51 = 0.73. (Lower loss = higher confidence in correct answer.)
The model learns: boost the probability of correct answers. Same training as language models.

math.note: This equation is identical to language model training, which is why vision-language knowledge survives; the difference is the masking schedule, which adds iterative refinement without changing the learning signal.

bars.h2: Comparison: old approaches vs. this paper

charts.title: Autoregressive (old VLA)
charts.note: Left-to-right decoding guesses blindly; later actions corroded by early errors.

charts.title: Continuous diffusion head (bolted on)
charts.note: Separate diffusion head competes with VLM objective; vision-language skills degrade on hard tests.

charts.title: This paper: Discrete Diffusion inside VLM
charts.note: Iterative refinement inside the backbone, same loss objective, preserves vision-language understanding.

items.html: Converting continuous action values (e.g. arm position 5.3 cm) to discrete tokens (bin 5) throws away sub-bin detail, causing errors on tasks that require fine positioning. The paper shows 0.7% performance loss from binning alone compared to continuous methods. Higher resolution bins (more possible values) reduce error but require the model to predict from a larger set of options, which costs more computation and slower inference.

If the schedule unmasks too fast, hard action dimensions get refined with little context. If too slow, inference takes many forward passes and becomes slow. The paper finds the right schedule by trial and error but does not give a principled method to set schedules for new domains.
If the model keeps detecting contradictions and re-masking, inference becomes unpredictably expensive. The paper does not define when to stop re-masking.

items.b: Done right: inherits biases from pretraining.
items.html: Because the method relies on a large pretrained vision-language model, it also inherits any biases in that model's training data. This is not unique to this paper but must be checked before real-world deployment (e.g. does the model underperform with certain arm poses or on certain objects?).

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a toy robot task: a robot arm must pick up one object from a table and place it in a bin, following a language instruction. Use a simple simulated arm with 3 continuous action dimensions (x, y, z position). Collect 50 human demonstrations. Train three variants: (1) autoregressive baseline (predict actions left to right), (2) continuous diffusion (separate head), (3) this paper (discrete diffusion inside the transformer). On a held-out test set of 20 new objects and instructions, measure success rate and how well the model follows instruction language after fine-tuning on the new objects.
demo.metric_eq: success_rate = (# of trajectories that pick up correct object and place in correct bin) / (# of test trials); language_retention = (accuracy on language paraphrases of instructions) before vs after fine-tuning
demo.closing: The demo is a success if: (1) discrete diffusion matches or exceeds continuous diffusion on the base task (success rate), because both should solve the task well, AND (2) when fine-tuned on new objects, the discrete method retains language understanding better than the continuous diffusion baseline (language retention gap < 5% vs >10% for continuous), because the discrete method uses the same training loss as the original vision-language model and does not dilute that objective with competing diffusion signals.
